new_value: • Correct Answer A (Bactria): In the early second century BC (around 190–180 BC), Demetrius I, ruler of the Greco-Bactrian kingdom centered in northern Afghanistan (the fertile Oxus river basin), pushed south across the Hindu Kush into the northwestern Indian subcontinent, establishing the Indo-Greek realm. • Why B is incorrect: Scythia refers to the domain of the nomadic Indo-Scythians (Sakas), who entered India later (around the 1st century BC) and displaced Indo-Greek rule, rather than establishing the original Greek kingdom. • Why C is incorrect: Zedrasia (Gedrosia) was the arid coastal satrapy corresponding to modern Makran/Balochistan in southwestern Pakistan and southeastern Iran, far south of northern Afghanistan. • Why D is incorrect: Aria was an ancient satrapy centered around the Hari River valley (modern Herat in western Afghanistan), not the power base of northern Afghanistan where the Indo-Greek state originated. • Often confused with: Greco-Bactrian Kingdom vs. Indo-Greek Kingdom — Greco-Bactria was the original Hellenistic state strictly north of the Hindu Kush, whereas the term Indo-Greeks specifically designates the Hellenistic rulers who expanded south of the Hindu Kush into Gandhara and the Punjab.
issues_found: Option C contains an archaic or corrupted spelling ('Zedrasia' instead of 'Gedrosia').

Historically, Bactria itself is the Greco-Bactrian home territory; the question conflates the geographical region of northern Afghanistan (Bactria) with the resultant 'Indo-Greek' kingdoms south of the Hindu Kush.
